question: What is different about how the sales team handles renewals versus new business?

resolution.read_instruction: Extract every statement and action by OrbitFlow sales staff describing how they run the call: opening and agenda, how they frame the purpose (renewal review vs new evaluation), discovery questions asked, demo or product focus, pricing, discounts, contract or term offers, commitments or promises made, urgency tactics, objection handling, and proposed next steps. Include the call type and the customer's stance where it bears on the sales team's approach.
assumptions: Comparison is between Renewal calls (CALL-011 to CALL-013) and Prospect calls (CALL-001 to CALL-010), as implied by 'renewals' and 'new business'.
Churn post-mortems and cold calls are excluded because the question names only renewals and new business.

findings.quote: my plan for today, roughly — I want to spend the first chunk just understanding how you actually handle this
findings.context: Call type is a new-business discovery and first demo for a prospect, not a renewal review. He disclosed the auto-renew notice deadline of 30 September. The customer said they would have not renewed before the call and trusted the proposal more for the candour.

claims.text: In new business, OrbitFlow routinely quotes Growth list pricing ($1,800/month, up to 30 users, annual) and steers larger prospects to custom Enterprise pricing. It often declines to give a firm number until the user model is known, and commits to an itemised proposal separating seats, volume and services (Acme, BrightPath, DeltaWorks, Greenline, Harbor Legal, Inkwell, Ember).

claims.text: New-business next steps are pilots, sandboxes, security packs and jointly written success criteria, often with the AE saying 'don't buy OrbitFlow' is a valid outcome (Acme, BrightPath). Examples: Ember got a six-week pilot with a timeline, and Juniper a four-week evaluation with a September go/no-go. evidence.speaker: Maya Chen

claims.text: Renewal commercial levers are retention-specific: Maya Chen at Lumen waived two overage charges, recommended cutting seats from nine to seven while raising the run tier to 400k, advised a two-year term over three, and promised a Friday proposal with one-, two- and three-year options priced separately.

evidence.speaker: Maya Chen
evidence.quote: Two were waived — one in March because it was a retry storm caused by a Salesforce outage on their side, and one in May which I waived because you'd flagged it to us proactively before the invoice.
evidence.context: The AE waived two of the overage charges as a goodwill concession, and says one waiver was a judgement call she is disclosing before the renewal. — Waivers used to manage overage invoices ahead of renewal, presented openly rather than discovered later.

evidence.speaker: Maya Chen
evidence.quote: I'd rather sell you seven active seats and a higher run tier than nine seats where four are indefensible.
evidence.context: The AE recommends cutting seats from nine to seven and raising the run tier, arguing this is better for the customer than keeping shelfware seats. — Upsell of run tier paired with a seat reduction. The AE frames the seat cut as genuine, not a way to inflate the run tier.

evidence.speaker: Maya Chen
evidence.quote: I think you should take four hundred, and I'd rather say that than sell you three fifty and have this conversation again in May.
evidence.context: The AE pushes the customer to the larger 400k run tier rather than the 350k tier, arguing the cheaper option would lead to a second renewal conversation sooner. — Upsell and tier recommendation. Her stated reason is avoiding a repeat conversation in May, not the customer's immediate need.

evidence.speaker: Maya Chen
evidence.quote: I'd do three. Should you? Probably not.
evidence.context: The AE says she would personally choose a three-year term but advises the customer to take two years, citing lock-in risk. — Term-length guidance. She advises against the longer commitment that she herself would prefer, which reads as a less self-interested steer.

evidence.speaker: Maya Chen
evidence.quote: A two-year commitment lets me fix the uplift for year two, which given where inflation's gone is probably worth more than the discount itself.
evidence.context: The AE presents a two-year term mainly as a way to fix the year-two uplift, and declines to give a discount figure without modelling it. — Multi-year offer. The value is framed around price protection, and the AE will not quote a discount on the spot.

evidence.speaker: Maya Chen
evidence.quote: Yes, and I'll show last year's line items next to next year's so you can see exactly what moved.
evidence.context: The AE commits to sending a line-by-line comparison of current and next-year pricing, and to showing the seat reduction separately so the customer can take it to finance. — Transparency offered to support the customer's internal approval process. The customer had said a finance director would ask what changed.

evidence.speaker: Maya Chen
evidence.quote: What you'll get from me by Friday is the renewal proposal with last year's line items next to next year's, seven seats, four hundred thousand runs, and one-year, two-year and three-year options priced separately.
evidence.context: The AE sets out next steps and a Friday deadline for a written renewal proposal with one-, two- and three-year options priced separately. — Proposed next steps. No binding agreement reached on the call.

He disclosed the auto-renew notice deadline of 30 September. The customer said they would have not renewed before the call and trusted the proposal more for the candour.

evidence.quote: Option one, you don't renew. We part on good terms, you export your workflow definitions and run data

evidence.speaker: Leo Grant
evidence.quote: Six months at the annual rate pro-rata, not at a short-term premium. So no uplift, no penalty for the shorter term. That's the concession.
evidence.context: Vendor (AE Leo) said the six-month term would be priced pro-rata at the annual rate with no short-term premium or uplift, and presented this as the concession. — Pricing and discount for the shorter renewal term. No discount was offered beyond removing the short-term premium.

evidence.speaker: Leo Grant
evidence.quote: Enablement included, not charged as professional services.
evidence.context: Vendor (AE Leo) committed to enablement at no charge, stating it would normally be billed as professional services. — Enablement is a bundled concession in the renewal offer, given to address an adoption problem the vendor said it partly caused.

evidence.speaker: Ruth Adeyemi
evidence.quote: For the six months, I'd want a fortnightly fifteen-minute call with Nadia. Not a QBR.
evidence.context: Vendor (CSM Ruth) proposed a standing fortnightly 15-minute check-in during the six-month term, explicitly not a QBR. — Account-management cadence proposed for the renewal period, positioned as a replacement for a QBR.

evidence.speaker: Leo Grant
evidence.quote: Your current contract auto-renews with sixty days' notice, which means your notice deadline is the thirtieth of September.
evidence.context: Vendor (AE Leo) told the customer about the auto-renew clause and its notice deadline, and advised them to serve notice to stop the auto-renew. — Vendor surfaced a contract deadline the customer had not known about and said it would not auto-renew the customer into a 12-month term. Leo described auto-renew as a practice some vendors use and called it a terrible way to run a business.

evidence.speaker: Graham Attwood
evidence.quote: If you'd asked me two weeks ago I'd have said we're not renewing.
evidence.context: Customer said that before this call they would have chosen not to renew, and that the vendor's candour about its own interest made them trust the rest of the proposal more. — Customer stance on the renewal. Inferred to be a meaningful influence on the approach. Customer had also said the review was more useful than expected.

evidence.speaker: Maya Chen
evidence.quote: What's the thing we do that you'd miss most if it vanished tomorrow?
evidence.context: The AE asks an open discovery question about what the customer values most, outside the renewal itself. — Discovery on a renewal call, used to surface value drivers for future selling rather than to close the renewal.

evidence.speaker: Ruth Adeyemi
evidence.quote: One question, and it's for my benefit rather than yours. Eighteen months in — what's the thing that's worked best?
evidence.context: Ruth asked the customer what had worked best after eighteen months, explicitly for her own benefit, as a renewal check-in question. — Discovery-style account health question at renewal. Customer answered with the onboarding workflow, which dropped client go-live from eleven days to four.

evidence.speaker: Ruth Adeyemi
evidence.quote: It's never been a problem yet. But you're a security company with no change control on production automation, and I'd rather point that out than have your own auditor point it out.
evidence.context: Ruth raised a governance gap (no defined promotion process for production) unprompted, saying she would rather point it out than have the customer's auditor do so. — Proactive account-management and upsell-style raise during a renewal. The customer had not previously considered it, and it was framed as an opportunity rather than a sales pitch.

evidence.speaker: Ruth Adeyemi
evidence.quote: It's thirty days for your contract. I checked before the call because I assumed you'd ask.
evidence.context: Ruth checked the contract's notice period before the call so she could answer the customer's question about subprocessor changes. — Account-management preparation for a renewal customer. The customer praised it.
